name: Tirzepatide

lead: Tirzepatide is a weekly injectable sold as Mounjaro and Zepbound. People use it to cut body fat, and the face leans out as weight comes off.

It activates both GIP and GLP-1 receptors, which lowers appetite and calorie intake. In the SURMOUNT-1 trial, average weight change at 72 weeks was about -15.0, -19.5 and -20.9 percent across the three studied strengths, among the largest reductions reported for an approved anti-obesity drug. Facial leaning follows total fat loss, and with larger losses, facial volume loss and skin laxity can be more noticeable in some users.

paras: It is prescribed as a once-weekly injection, with the amount stepped up gradually by the prescriber. Users combine it with high protein intake and resistance training to preserve muscle. Results build over months, and weight returns after stopping.

Nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea and constipation are common, mostly while the amount is being increased. Pancreatitis, gallbladder disease and dehydration-related kidney injury have been reported, and the label carries a thyroid C-cell tumour warning. It can reduce the effectiveness of oral contraceptives. Lean mass is lost along with fat. It is prescription-only; unregulated peptide-vial sources add contamination and accuracy risks.

angle.text: Users take tirzepatide to cut body fat, with strong appetite suppression creating a larger calorie deficit and a leaner body and face. Trials show some of the largest weight losses of any approved drug; facial leanness and muscle retention are discussed mainly by users.

lead: Tirzepatide is an injectable peptide that activates both the glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide (GIP) receptor and the glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor. Made by Eli Lilly, it is given once weekly and sold as Mounjaro for type 2 diabetes and as Zepbound for chronic weight management and, in the United States, moderate-to-severe obstructive sleep apnea [1][2].

In the SURMOUNT-1 phase 3 trial of adults with obesity or overweight without diabetes, mean weight change at 72 weeks was about -15.0, -19.5 and -20.9 percent at the 5, 10 and 15 mg weekly doses [1][3]. These are among the largest average reductions reported for an approved anti-obesity drug, and in a 2025 head-to-head trial it was compared directly with semaglutide [4].

Looksmaxxing communities discuss tirzepatide as a systemic fat-loss tool; facial leaning follows overall fat loss rather than being targeted. Its documented adverse effects are mostly gastrointestinal, and the US label carries a boxed warning on thyroid C-cell tumors observed in rodents [2]. Weight regain after stopping is documented, and forum users also discuss unregulated peptide supplies, whose contents are not verified by regulators.

paras: Mounjaro is indicated as an adjunct to diet and exercise to improve glycemic control in adults with type 2 diabetes, and the US label extends this to pediatric patients aged 10 and above [2]. Zepbound is indicated alongside a reduced-calorie diet and increased physical activity for long-term weight reduction in adults with obesity, or overweight with at least one weight-related condition, and for moderate-to-severe obstructive sleep apnea in adults with obesity [1]. The FDA approved the sleep apnea indication in December 2024 [1].

Appearance-focused users take tirzepatide to lose body fat through appetite reduction. It has no known mechanism for removing facial fat selectively; changes to the face are described as following total fat loss, and forum members who report on the drug describe strong hunger suppression [5][6]. The larger average weight loss compared with older drugs means that facial volume loss may be more noticeable in some people, according to forum discussion, although no trial has studied facial appearance.

SURMOUNT-1 randomized 2,539 adults with a BMI of 30 or higher, or 27 or higher with a weight-related complication and no diabetes, to weekly tirzepatide or placebo for 72 weeks [3]. A three-year follow-up reported safety outcomes and effects on progression to type 2 diabetes in people with obesity and prediabetes [7]. In people with type 2 diabetes and obesity, SURMOUNT-2 tested the drug against placebo [8].

In the SURPASS-2 trial in type 2 diabetes, tirzepatide at 5, 10 and 15 mg was compared with semaglutide over 40 weeks [9], and network meta-analyses have compared tirzepatide with semaglutide and other GLP-1 drugs on blood glucose and body weight [10][11]. A 2025 head-to-head trial in obesity without diabetes compared the maximum tolerated doses of the two drugs in an open-label design [4].

Body composition has been reported in a SURMOUNT-1 substudy [12]. A 2025 network meta-analysis of 22 randomized trials found that GLP-1 receptor agonists and dual agonists reduced fat mass and lean mass, with lean mass about a quarter of the total loss across the class [13].

Maintenance and discontinuation have been studied. SURMOUNT-4 randomized participants who had lost weight on tirzepatide either to continue or to switch to placebo [14]. Wikipedia reports that participants regained on average about 53 percent of their lost weight within a year of stopping, and a 2025 meta-analysis of GLP-1 drugs examined weight after discontinuation [1][15].

The most common adverse effects are nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, decreased appetite, constipation and abdominal discomfort or pain, which mostly occur during dose escalation and increase with dose [1]. In the 2018 phase 2 diabetes trial summarized by Wikipedia, 25 percent of participants on the 15 mg dose discontinued compared with 5.1 percent on 5 mg [1].

The US label carries a boxed warning for thyroid C-cell tumors in rodents and contraindicates the drug in people with a personal or family history of medullary thyroid carcinoma or multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2 [2]. Other labelled warnings include acute pancreatitis, hypoglycemia with insulin or insulin secretagogues, hypersensitivity reactions, acute kidney injury from volume depletion and severe gastrointestinal reactions [2]. The label says pregnancy data are insufficient and animal studies show possible fetal risk [2]. A pharmacovigilance analysis of reports to the FDA Adverse Event Reporting System has also examined tirzepatide signals [16]. A large meta-analysis of GLP-1 receptor agonist trials assessed mortality, cardiovascular events and serious adverse events across the class [17].

Tirzepatide selectively activates the GIP and GLP-1 receptors. It is more potent than native GIP at the GIP receptor, while at the GLP-1 receptor it shows bias toward cAMP signaling over beta-arrestin recruitment [1][2]. GLP-1 activity reduces appetite and slows gastric emptying; the added role of GIP agonism is under study. The label states that tirzepatide enhances first- and second-phase insulin secretion and reduces glucagon in a glucose-dependent manner [2]. Wikipedia reports increases in adiponectin of up to 26 percent after 26 weeks at 10 mg [1]. A 2026 meta-analysis reported reductions in inflammatory markers hsCRP and IL-6 versus placebo [18].

Tirzepatide is a modified analog of human GIP with a C20 fatty diacid attached via a linker to a lysine side chain; the fatty acid binds albumin and prolongs half-life to about five days, allowing weekly dosing [1][19][2].

Eli Lilly first applied for a patent on a method of glycemic control using tirzepatide in 2016 and filed for FDA approval in 2021 with a priority review voucher [1]. The FDA approved Mounjaro for type 2 diabetes in May 2022, the European Union followed in September 2022, and Zepbound was approved for weight management in November 2023 and for obstructive sleep apnea in December 2024 [1][19]. Lilly announced in April 2022 that phase 3 results in people with overweight or obesity without diabetes met their endpoints [1].

Bodybuilding and appearance forums discuss tirzepatide alongside testosterone therapy, other peptides and dieting. T Nation members describe using or planning to use it for cutting and to curb appetite, and one clinic owner lists weight-loss injections as part of a service mix [20][21][22][23]. A looksmax.org post in a long personal guide covers tirzepatide in a section on fat loss [24]. Some posters compare it with retatrutide, saying the latter is better for fat loss and tirzepatide for hunger control [5][25]. Members also mention insurance not covering the drugs and the existence of compounded supply [21].

Tirzepatide has been evaluated in a large randomized trial program. For obesity, SURMOUNT-1 (with a three-year extension), SURMOUNT-2 (type 2 diabetes), SURMOUNT-4 (maintenance) and the sleep apnea trials are principal publications [3][7][8][14][26]. SURPASS trials, including SURPASS-2 against semaglutide, tested it in type 2 diabetes [9]. Other randomized trials examined heart failure with preserved ejection fraction and obesity [27] and steatohepatitis with fibrosis [28], and a 2025 trial compared it with semaglutide in obesity [4]. Registered studies are exploring further conditions, including central centrifugal cicatricial alopecia [29]. No published trial has tested tirzepatide for facial appearance.

lore.intro: Tirzepatide is discussed on bodybuilding and appearance forums as the strongest available appetite-control drug, often compared with semaglutide and retatrutide [5][25].

claims.claim: Tirzepatide is more effective for fat loss than semaglutide.
It strongly suppresses hunger, making a cut easier.
The weight loss stops showing in the mirror or damages metabolism.
Small doses of the drug are enough for lean users.
Compounded or research-peptide tirzepatide is a practical alternative to prescription supply.
